To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) mitochondrial Ca2+ accumulation occurs in the presence of physiological concentrations of Ca2+ and Mg2+; (2) mitochondrial Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release occurs in the presence, but not in the absence, of physiological concentrations of Mg2+; and (3) mitochondrial Ca2+/Mg2+-dependent release of Ca2+ is a mechanism that is activated under pathological conditions, but is not normally involved in control of metabolism.

the Na+-independent and the Na+-dependent mechanisms of mitochondrial Ca(2+) transport are regulated in opposite directions by intramitochondrially generated ATP, that the Na+-dependent Ca(2+) transporter is regulated by the pH gradient across the inner membrane, and that the two Ca2+ transport systems are both involved in the permeability transition.
mitochondrial Ca2+ influx is a major determinant of cell death, and that mitochondrial Ca2+-induced permeability transition is a major cause of mitochondrial Ca2+-dependent cell death.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of mitochondrial calcium transport and the physiological and pathological consequences of mitochondrial calcium accumulation.
the physiological role and pathological relevance of the mitochondrial Ca(2+) transport systems.

the mechanisms by which mitochondria take up and release calcium, the physiological role of these mechanisms in the regulation of cellular metabolism and the pathological role of the mitochondrial Ca(2+) transport mechanisms in cell death.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while there are many unanswered questions, there is now a strong and coherent case that mitochondrial Ca2+ is a physiological regulator of metabolism.

there is a strong circumstantial case for the physiological importance of the mitochondrial Ca(2+) transport mechanisms, but that the case for a role of intramitochondial Ca2+ in the control of metabolism is not as strong.

there is a strong case for mitochondrial Ca2+ sequestration in the regulation of metabolism, but that the evidence is not as strong for a role for mitochondrial Ca2+-induced permeability transition in irreversible cell damage, although the possibility cannot be excluded.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mitochondrial Na+ independent and Na+ dependent Ca2+ transporters are not simply energy-consuming pumps but have physiological roles in regulating mitochondrial Ca2+ and, in turn, metabolism.
there is a good understanding of the mechanisms of the mitochondrial Ca 2+ transporters, but little is known about the physiological and pathological relevance of mitochondrial Ca2+.
there is a strong physiological rationale for mitochondrial Ca2+ sequestration, and that the mechanisms are consistent with a role in control of metabolism and in cell damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the physiological role of mitochondrial Ca2+, if there is one, remains enigmatic.
the mitochondrial Ca2+-transporting mechanisms are highly regulated and have evolved to be able to function under conditions of high Ca2+ load.

there is a strong physiological rationale for mitochondrial Ca2+ sequestration, but that the mechanisms of Ca2+ transport have evolved to serve this purpose in a way that is not always compatible with the requirements of other cellular functions.
